text: If the tests keep coming back normal while that investigation goes on, I'd also try one of the two talk therapies I go into in [my somatic guide](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/201523223/pain-that-wont-quit), Pain Reprocessing Therapy or Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy. They both treat the pain as real, and they've helped people with long-lasting back, muscle and joint pain.
reader: an adult with pain attacks that tests keep explaining away, reading the inner child guide's Physical Pain section, deciding what to try while the doctors keep looking

checked.point: both therapies tell patients the pain is real, made by the brain
checked.found: VA Eastern Colorado, "All Pain is Real" (https://www.va.gov/eastern-colorado-health-care/programs/understanding-chronic-pain-what-you-need-to-know/); Lumley and Schubiner 2019, EAET for chronic pain (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7309024): the brain generates or amplifies primary pain
checked.still_needed: yes: they hear the guide is not calling their pain imaginary

checked.point: PRT: reappraisal of pain sensations and of the beliefs that the pain means harm; a graded return to feared activities; mild to moderate chronic back pain; 66% vs 20% pain-free or nearly, gains largely held at one year
checked.found: Ashar et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry 79(1):13-23 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8482298): "guided reappraisal of pain sensations", "fear- and avoidance-inducing beliefs"; NIH Research Matters, 2021-11-02
checked.still_needed: yes: they weigh it for their own pain

checked.point: EAET: emotional expression and role-play of hard conversations; 126 veterans aged 60 to 95 with muscle and joint pain; 63% vs 17% with at least 30% less pain
checked.found: Yarns et al. 2024, JAMA Network Open (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03918642)
checked.still_needed: yes: they weigh it for their own pain and age

placement: a paragraph of its own at the end of Physical Pain?, after his advice not to stop the investigation

Part of how you learn it is by paying close attention to how the pain feels in your body.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
